title: Failures too
hookLine: Muslim history includes cruelty and injustice, and the tradition itself criticizes it

cards: Who wrote down the day of Karbala? Not an enemy of Islam. Muslim historians did, al-Tabari among them, and they set down in plain detail an army of a Muslim ruler killing the Prophet's own grandson and many of his family.
Names, speeches, who struck whom. They didn't bury it. They copied it, taught it and argued over it.
This path has told a lot of history this year with admiration. Today it turns the other way, and asks what the tradition does with its own worst days. Today: failures too.

teach.b: There were cruel rulers. Unjust wars. Prisoners mistreated, scholars jailed, the poor taxed to pay for palaces.
Muslim history holds all of that, the way every long human history does. The surprise is where the sharpest criticism came from: inside. First, the standard.
The Qur'an asks believers to tell the truth even when it costs their own side.

teach.h: STAUNCH IN JUSTICE, EVEN AGAINST YOURSELVES.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred."
Against yourselves: your own dynasty, your own history. Second, the voice.

teach.h: A WORD OF JUSTICE BEFORE A TYRANT.
teach.b: A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud calls a word of justice spoken before an unjust ruler the best kind of striving. Third, the people who paid for it.

The scholar Ahmad ibn Hanbal was imprisoned and beaten under the caliph's officials for refusing to say what the court required. Hasan al-Basri, whom we met earlier, admonished the governors of his day.
Their students kept their names and honored them; the officials who did the beating are mostly footnotes. Fourth, the mirror.

teach.h: OUR LORD, WE HAVE WRONGED OURSELVES.
teach.b: In the Qur'an, Adam and his wife did wrong in the garden, and their answer is the model of an honest believer, in Pickthall's words: "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves." No excuses, no blaming the other.
The faith is strong enough to name its failures, and so is a person.

how: Muslims seek forgiveness (istighfar) from God daily, and the tradition teaches that wronging another person also requires putting it right with that person.

o: a list of the battles Muslim armies lost
a history honest enough to name its wrongs
the idea that the faith itself has failed

p: wrote down the day of Karbala
imprisoned and beaten, would not yield

s: Muslim historians left Karbala out of their histories
al-Tabari and others set it down in detail.
the Qur'an asks for justice even against yourselves and your kin
"be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred."
Adam and his wife blamed each other after the garden
their words in the Qur'an are "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves."

games.q: you're a scholar summoned to court. the caliph's officials want you to say something you believe is false. refusing means prison. what do you do?
o: say it; the ruler's word settles it.
say it now and take it back once you're free.
games.why: Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused, and was imprisoned and beaten. his students remembered him, not the officials.

practice: Let one real thing you got wrong come up, not the worst thing you've ever done, just one: a sharp word, a promise dropped, a time you took the easy side.
Look at it straight, the way those historians looked at Karbala, without dressing it up and without beating yourself with it, and say it in one plain sentence: I did this.
If you pray, you can say the words of Adam and his wife: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves.

wordCard.voice: Failures too. Muslim history holds cruelty and injustice, and the tradition's own scholars and historians named them. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: wrongdoing, injustice. the same root is in "we have wronged ourselves" (7:23).

carryVoice: Your line: honesty is faith. Name it plainly, and without cruelty to yourself. Same time tomorrow.
